items.title: Evaluating a Double Integral Using the Multiplicative Property

sections.normalized_html: Evaluate the double integral [MATH: \displaystyle \iint\limits_{R} xy\ \!e^{x+y}\ \textrm d A] over the rectangle [MATH: R= [0,1] \times [1,2].]
sections.readable_text: Evaluate the double integral [MATH: \displaystyle \iint\limits_{R} xy\ \!e^{x+y}\ \textrm d A] over the rectangle [MATH: R= [0,1] \times [1,2].]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
We apply the multiplicative property of double integrals and then evaluate each of the integrals separately:
[MATH: \eqalign{ \iint\limits_{R} xy\ e^{x+y}\: \textrm d A &= \iint\limits_{R} \Big( x\ \! e^x \Big)\Big( y\ \! e^{y} \Big) \textrm d A\[5pt] &= \left(\int_0^1x\ e^{x} \ \textrm d x\right)\left( \int_1^2 y \ \!e^{y} \ \textrm d y\right)\[5pt] &= \Big[x\ \!e^x-e^x\Big]_0^1 \cdot \Big[y\ \!e^y-e^y\Big]_1^2\[5pt] &= \Big(e^1-e^1 - \left(0-e^0\right)\Big) \cdot \Big(2e^2-e^2 - \left(e^1-e^1\right) \Big)\[5pt] &= 1\cdot e^2\[5pt] &= e^2 }]
sections.readable_text:
We apply the multiplicative property of double integrals and then evaluate each of the integrals separately:
[MATH: \eqalign{
\iint\limits_{R} xy\ e^{x+y}\: \textrm d A &= \iint\limits_{R} \Big( x\ \! e^x \Big)\Big( y\ \! e^{y} \Big) \textrm d A\[5pt]
&= \left(\int_0^1x\ e^{x} \ \textrm d x\right)\left( \int_1^2 y \ \!e^{y} \ \textrm d y\right)\[5pt]
&= \Big[x\ \!e^x-e^x\Big]_0^1 \cdot \Big[y\ \!e^y-e^y\Big]_1^2\[5pt]
&= \Big(e^1-e^1 - \left(0-e^0\right)\Big) \cdot \Big(2e^2-e^2 - \left(e^1-e^1\right) \Big)\[5pt]
&= 1\cdot e^2\[5pt]
&= e^2
}]

items.readable_text:
Example Prompt:
Evaluate the double integral [MATH: \displaystyle \iint\limits_{R} xy\ \!e^{x+y}\ \textrm d A] over the rectangle [MATH: R= [0,1] \times [1,2].]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We apply the multiplicative property of double integrals and then evaluate each of the integrals separately:
[MATH: \eqalign{
\iint\limits_{R} xy\ e^{x+y}\: \textrm d A &= \iint\limits_{R} \Big( x\ \! e^x \Big)\Big( y\ \! e^{y} \Big) \textrm d A\[5pt]
&= \left(\int_0^1x\ e^{x} \ \textrm d x\right)\left( \int_1^2 y \ \!e^{y} \ \textrm d y\right)\[5pt]
&= \Big[x\ \!e^x-e^x\Big]_0^1 \cdot \Big[y\ \!e^y-e^y\Big]_1^2\[5pt]
&= \Big(e^1-e^1 - \left(0-e^0\right)\Big) \cdot \Big(2e^2-e^2 - \left(e^1-e^1\right) \Big)\[5pt]
&= 1\cdot e^2\[5pt]
&= e^2
}]

sections.normalized_html: Calculate [MATH: \displaystyle \iint\limits_{R} \left(x^2-y^2 +3\right) \textrm d A,] where [MATH: R= [-1,3] \times [2, 4].]
sections.readable_text: Calculate [MATH: \displaystyle \iint\limits_{R} \left(x^2-y^2 +3\right) \textrm d A,] where [MATH: R= [-1,3] \times [2, 4].]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Using the linearity property of double integrals, we can write [MATH: ∬_(R)(x^{2} − y^{2} + 3)dA|= ∬_(R)x^{2}dA − ∬_(R)y^{2}dA + ∬_(R)3dA.]

Now, let's evaluate each of the three integrals.

  • The function under the first integral is independent of [MATH: y.] So, we have [MATH: ∬_(R)x^{2}dA|= (4 − 2)∫_{− 1}^{3}x^{2}dx; = 2 ⋅ (x^{3})/(3)|_{− 1}^{3}; = 2((27)/(3) + (1)/(3)); = (56)/(3).]

  • The function under the second integral is independent of [MATH: x.] So, we have
    [MATH: ∬_(R)y^{2}dA|= (3 − (− 1))∫_{2}^{4}y^{2}dy; = 4∫_{2}^{4}y^{2}dy; = 4 ⋅ (y^{3})/(3)|_{2}^{4}; = (4)/(3)4^{3} − (4)/(3)2^{3}; = (224)/(3).]

  • The function under the third integral is a constant, so we have [MATH: ∬_(R)3dA = 3Area(R) = 3 ⋅ (2 ⋅ 4) = 24.]

Finally, combining our results, we obtain

[MATH: ∬_(R)(x^{2} − y^{2} + 3)dA = (56)/(3) − (224)/(3) + 24 = − 32.]

In the same way, the definite integral of a two-variable function can be split up over adjacent sub-domains.

items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose that we're integrating a single-variable function over a region [MATH: R.] The definite integral of [MATH: f(x)] over [MATH: R] is not affected by whether the region [MATH: R] is open or closed.

Content:
For example, consider the function [MATH: f(x) = 1,] and define the regions [MATH: R = [0,1]] and [MATH: R' = (0,1).] Integrating [MATH: f(x)] over [MATH: R] and [MATH: R'] gives the same result:

Content:
[MATH: \int_R f(x) \,\textrm d x = \int_{R'} f(x) \,\textrm d x = \int_{0}^1 \,\textrm d x = 1]

Content:
Intuitively, this is true because the rectangles formed by [MATH: f(x),] namely [MATH: [0, 1]\times [0,1]] and [MATH: (0, 1)\times (0,1),] have the same area.

Content:
We have a similar property for double integrals too. We can either include or exclude the boundaries of the integration regions without affecting the result.

Content:
For example, the double integral of [MATH: f(x,y)=x^2+y^2] over both [MATH: R=[0,1] \times [0,1]] and over [MATH: R'=(0,1) \times (0,1)] will give the same result:

Content:
[MATH: \iint\limits_{\large R} (x^2+y^2) \ \text{d}A = \iint\limits_{\large R'} (x^2+y^2) \ \text{d}A= \int_{0}^{1} \int_{0}^{1} (x^2+y^2) \ \text{d}A]

Content:
Intuitively, this is true because the volumes of the shapes formed by [MATH: f(x,y)] over the regions [MATH: R] and [MATH: R'] are the same.

Content:
Moreover, we'd get the same result if we were to integrate [MATH: f(x,y)] over any of the following regions:

Content:
[MATH: (0,1] \times [0,1], \quad [0,1) \times [0,1], \quad (0,1) \times [0,1], \quad \ldots]

Content:
The same idea applies to double-integrals over non-rectangular boundaries, too.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Double integrals have properties that are similar to the properties of definite integrals of single-variable functions:

Content:
- Linearity of Double Integrals. Suppose that [MATH: f(x,y)] and [MATH: g(x,y)] are continuous functions on a domain [MATH: D] and that [MATH: \alpha, \beta] are constants. Then, we have
[MATH: \iint\limits_{D} \left[\alpha f(x,y) + \beta g(x,y)\right] \ \textrm d A = \alpha\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \textrm d A + \beta\iint\limits_{D} g(x,y) \ \textrm d A.]
- The Double Integral of Unity. The integral of [MATH: f(x,y) = 1] over a domain [MATH: D] is simply the area of [MATH: D\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: \displaystyle \iint\limits_{D} \ \textrm d A = \displaystyle \iint\limits_{D} 1 \cdot \textrm d A = \textrm{Area}\ \!(D).]

Content:
Other properties are more specific to double integrals.

Content:
- The Multiplicative Property of Double Integrals. If [MATH: f(x)] is continuous on [MATH: [a,b]] and [MATH: g(y)] is continuous on [MATH: [c,d]] then
[MATH: \iint\limits_{R} f(x)g(y) \ \textrm d A = \left(\int_a^b f(x) \ \textrm d x\right)\left( \int_c^d g(y) \ \textrm d y\right),]
where [MATH: R= [a,b] \times [c,d].]

---

Item 2 — Example: Evaluating a Double Integral Using the Multiplicative Property

Example Prompt:
Evaluate the double integral [MATH: \displaystyle \iint\limits_{R} xy\ \!e^{x+y}\ \textrm d A] over the rectangle [MATH: R= [0,1] \times [1,2].]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We apply the multiplicative property of double integrals and then evaluate each of the integrals separately:
[MATH: \eqalign{
\iint\limits_{R} xy\ e^{x+y}\: \textrm d A &= \iint\limits_{R} \Big( x\ \! e^x \Big)\Big( y\ \! e^{y} \Big) \textrm d A\[5pt]
&= \left(\int_0^1x\ e^{x} \ \textrm d x\right)\left( \int_1^2 y \ \!e^{y} \ \textrm d y\right)\[5pt]
&= \Big[x\ \!e^x-e^x\Big]_0^1 \cdot \Big[y\ \!e^y-e^y\Big]_1^2\[5pt]
&= \Big(e^1-e^1 - \left(0-e^0\right)\Big) \cdot \Big(2e^2-e^2 - \left(e^1-e^1\right) \Big)\[5pt]
&= 1\cdot e^2\[5pt]
&= e^2
}]

---

Item 5 — Tutorial: Applying the Multiplicative Property when the Integrand Contains Only One Variable

Content:
We can also apply the multiplicative property when the integrand contains only one of the variables.

Content:
For example, suppose that [MATH: R= [a,b] \times [c,d].] Then, we have the general result

Content:
[MATH: ∬_(R)f(x)dA|= ∬_(R)(f(x))(1)dA; = (∫_{a}^{b}f(x)dx)(∫_{c}^{d}1dy); = (∫_{a}^{b}f(x)dx)(d − c); = (d − c)∫_{a}^{b}f(x)dx.]

Content:
By the same reasoning, we also have

Content:
[MATH: \iint\limits_{R} g(y) \, \textrm{d}A = (b-a) \int_c^d g(y) \, \textrm{d}y.]

---

Item 6 — Example: Evaluating a Double Integral When the Integrand Contains Only One Variable

Example Prompt:
Calculate [MATH: \displaystyle \iint\limits_{R} \left(x^2-y^2 +3\right) \textrm d A,] where [MATH: R= [-1,3] \times [2, 4].]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Using the linearity property of double integrals, we can write
[MATH: ∬_(R)(x^{2} − y^{2} + 3)dA|= ∬_(R)x^{2}dA − ∬_(R)y^{2}dA + ∬_(R)3dA.]

Now, let's evaluate each of the three integrals.

- The function under the first integral is independent of [MATH: y.] So, we have
[MATH: ∬_(R)x^{2}dA|= (4 − 2)∫_{− 1}^{3}x^{2}dx; = 2 ⋅ (x^{3})/(3)|_{− 1}^{3}; = 2((27)/(3) + (1)/(3)); = (56)/(3).]
- The function under the second integral is independent of [MATH: x.] So, we have
[MATH: ∬_(R)y^{2}dA|= (3 − (− 1))∫_{2}^{4}y^{2}dy; = 4∫_{2}^{4}y^{2}dy; = 4 ⋅ (y^{3})/(3)|_{2}^{4}; = (4)/(3)4^{3} − (4)/(3)2^{3}; = (224)/(3).]
- The function under the third integral is a constant, so we have
[MATH: ∬_(R)3dA = 3Area(R) = 3 ⋅ (2 ⋅ 4) = 24.]

Finally, combining our results, we obtain

[MATH: ∬_(R)(x^{2} − y^{2} + 3)dA = (56)/(3) − (224)/(3) + 24 = − 32.]

Item 9 — Tutorial: Additivity of Double Integrals

Content:
Remember that the definite integral of a single-variable function can be split up over adjacent subintervals. That is to say,

Content:
[MATH: \int_a^c f(x) \, \textrm dx = \int_a^b f(x) \, \textrm dx + \int_b^c f(x) \, \textrm dx.]

Content:
In the same way, the definite integral of a two-variable function can be split up over adjacent sub-domains.

Content:
Suppose that a domain [MATH: D] is the union of two adjacent sub-domains [MATH: D_1] and [MATH: D_2] (meaning that [MATH: D_1] and [MATH: D_2] are non-overlapping regions that could share a common border). Then, we have

Content:
[MATH: \iint\limits_{D} f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A = \iint\limits_{D_1} f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A + \iint\limits_{D_2} f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A.]

Content:
This property can be generalized if [MATH: D] is split into a finite number [MATH: n] of sub-domains (where [MATH: n>2]):

Content:
[MATH: \iint\limits_{D} f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A = \iint\limits_{D_1} f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A + \iint\limits_{D_2} f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A + \cdots + \iint\limits_{D_n} f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A]

---

Using the linearity and additivity of double integrals, we get the following:

[MATH: ∬_(C∪D)3f(x, y)dA|= 3∬_(C∪D)f(x, y)dA; = 3(∬_(C)f(x, y)dA + ∬_(D)f(x, y)dA); = 3(8 + (− 5)); = 3 ⋅ 3; = 9]

We have a similar property for double integrals too. We can either include or exclude the boundaries of the integration regions without affecting the result.

Content:
For example, the double integral of [MATH: f(x,y)=x^2+y^2] over both [MATH: R=[0,1] \times [0,1]] and over [MATH: R'=(0,1) \times (0,1)] will give the same result:

Content:
[MATH: \iint\limits_{\large R} (x^2+y^2) \ \text{d}A = \iint\limits_{\large R'} (x^2+y^2) \ \text{d}A= \int_{0}^{1} \int_{0}^{1} (x^2+y^2) \ \text{d}A]

Content:
Intuitively, this is true because the volumes of the shapes formed by [MATH: f(x,y)] over the regions [MATH: R] and [MATH: R'] are the same.

Content:
Moreover, we'd get the same result if we were to integrate [MATH: f(x,y)] over any of the following regions:

Content:
[MATH: (0,1] \times [0,1], \quad [0,1) \times [0,1], \quad (0,1) \times [0,1], \quad \ldots]

Content:
The same idea applies to double-integrals over non-rectangular boundaries, too.

Item 14 — Example: Evaluating a Double Integral Using the Additivity Over a Rectangular Domain

Example Prompt:
Evaluate the double integral [MATH: \displaystyle \iint\limits_{R} f(x,y)\ \textrm d A], where

[MATH: {2,|if0 < x < 2, − 1 < y < 0; (1)/(xy + x + y + 1),|if0 < x < 2, 0 < y < 1,]
and [MATH: R] is the domain of [MATH: f.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, notice that we have [MATH: R = R_1 \cup R_2,] where [MATH: R_1= (0,2) \times (-1,0)] and [MATH: R_2= (0,2) \times (0,1).] So, we can write

[MATH: \eqalign{
\iint\limits_{R} f(x,y)\ \textrm d A &= \iint\limits_{R_1} 2 \ \textrm d A + \iint\limits_{R_2} \dfrac{1}{xy+x+y+1} \ \textrm d A\[5pt]
&= 2\iint\limits_{R_1} \textrm d A
+ \iint\limits_{R_2} \dfrac{1}{(x+1)(y+1)} \ \textrm d A\[5pt]
&= 2(2-0)(0-(-1)) + \Bigg( \int_0^2 \dfrac{1}{x+1} \ \textrm d x \Bigg) \Bigg( \int_0^1 \dfrac{1}{y+1}\ \textrm d y \Bigg) \[5pt]
&= 4 + \Big[\ln(x+1)\Big]_0^2 \cdot \Big[\ln(y+1)\Big]_0^1\[5pt]
&= 4+ \ln 3\ln 2.
}]
